items.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002
items.q: Don Ewell... wound up playing duets with Willie “The Lion” Smith in New York

ctx.x: No, like the records that made “Shoeshine Boy” and all that. They had that kind of feel. And that grabbed me. Because on the other side of town they were playing Dixieland or whatever they called it. But there was a great pianist I used to follow around who made a big reputation, his name was Don Ewell. E-W-E-L-L. And his brother was a trombone player. They had a band that sounded like Bob Crosby’s Bobcats. A terrific band. But Don was brilliant — he wound up playing duets with Willie “The Lion” Smith in New York…

a contemporary, what was then contemporary. He used to sound a little like Teddy Wilson and Jess Stacey. That was contemporary when he came up. But then after the war he went back and he became like Jelly Roll Morton. He was not original but he was identifiable. In other words the idea is if you’re going to pick a style to play in, that’s okay, as long as you’re recognizable. Like Scott Hamilton. They thought he was crazy, you know, this kid coming around. In the meantime there’s Coltrane, and here’s this kid…
